items.prompt: Why doesn't being technically correct, by itself, make a piece of work read as "senior-level"?
choices: Because correctness is a baseline expectation for anyone whose code ships, not something that varies between a junior and senior contribution
Because correctness doesn't actually matter at all in performance reviews
Because only difficult problems count as correct
Because senior engineers are graded on a completely different, unrelated set of skills
items.reference:
✅ Correctness — a necessary baseline
📏 Scope — the variable that actually differs between a small fix and a senior-level one

Why: Priya and Sam were both correct — that column didn't distinguish their reviews at all.
items.explanation: Correctness is expected of everyone whose work ships — it's a baseline, not a differentiator. Priya and Sam were both correct, yet their reviews read very differently, which shows correctness alone doesn't explain the gap.

items.prompt: In the opening scenario, what was true of BOTH Priya's and Sam's diagnoses?
choices: Both were incorrect but caught in code review
Both were completely correct — no dispute, clean fixes, both merged without incident
Only Sam's diagnosis was correct
Neither diagnosis was ever verified
items.reference:
✅ Correctness — a necessary baseline
📏 Scope — the variable that actually differs between a small fix and a senior-level one

Why: Priya and Sam were both correct — that column didn't distinguish their reviews at all.
items.explanation: Both diagnoses were unambiguously correct — the scenario is explicit about this. The variable that differed between the two reviews was scope, not correctness.

items.prompt: How does this unit define "scope"?
choices: How difficult a piece of code was to write
The size of the blast radius a piece of work touches — how many users, systems, or dollars are involved
How many lines of code were changed
How long the task took to complete
items.reference:
📏 Scope — blast radius: users, systems, revenue, dependents
🎯 Independent of how hard the fix itself was

Why: Sam's fix was a single conditional check — easy to write, but large in scope because of what it prevented.
items.explanation: Scope is about blast radius — how far the consequences of a piece of work reach, measured in users, systems, revenue, or dependents — not about the difficulty of the code itself.

items.prompt: A one-line fix and a two-week refactor can, in principle, have the same scope. What would make that true?
choices: It can never be true — bigger code changes always have bigger scope
If both affect the same number of users, systems, or amount of revenue at risk, their scope is comparable regardless of how much code each required
Only if both took the same amount of time to write
Scope is always proportional to lines of code changed
items.reference:
📏 Scope — blast radius: users, systems, revenue, dependents
🎯 Independent of how hard the fix itself was

Why: Sam's fix was a single conditional check — easy to write, but large in scope because of what it prevented.
items.explanation: Scope tracks consequences, not code volume — a small fix and a large refactor can have identical scope if they affect the same number of users or amount of revenue, which is exactly why Sam's one-line fix outweighed a more "impressive-looking" change.

items.prompt: How does this unit define "impact", as distinct from scope?
choices: Impact and scope are exactly the same thing with no distinction
The realized or prevented consequence of the work — scope combined with how likely the bad outcome actually was to happen
Impact only refers to positive outcomes, never prevented ones
Impact is measured purely by how many people praised the work
items.reference:
📏 Scope — how far consequences could reach
💥 Impact — scope combined with actual likelihood of the bad outcome

Why: Sam's catch had both large scope (3,100 customers) and near-certain likelihood (the batch job was scheduled to run) — which is what made the impact real, not hypothetical.
items.explanation: Impact is scope combined with likelihood — it's the realized or prevented consequence, not just the theoretical size of what could have gone wrong.

items.prompt: Sam's bug catch is described as "prevented" impact rather than "realized" impact. What does that distinction mean?
choices: That the impact never actually happened because Sam caught it before the batch job ran, so the consequence is counted as avoided rather than experienced
That Sam's fix had no real impact since nothing bad actually occurred
That prevented impact never counts toward a performance review
That realized impact is always more valuable than prevented impact
items.reference:
📏 Scope — how far consequences could reach
💥 Impact — scope combined with actual likelihood of the bad outcome

Why: Sam's catch had both large scope (3,100 customers) and near-certain likelihood (the batch job was scheduled to run) — which is what made the impact real, not hypothetical.
items.explanation: "Prevented" impact means the bad outcome didn't happen precisely because someone caught it in advance — the $186,000 in erroneous charges was avoided, not absorbed, which is exactly why the unit argues prevention deserves as much credit as fixing something after it breaks.

items.prompt: What question does "blast radius" ask about a piece of work?
choices: How much time it will take to complete
If this had gone wrong, what exactly would have broken, and how far would it have spread?
How many people wrote code review comments on it
Whether the code passed all unit tests
items.reference:
💣 Blast radius — a concrete way to describe scope
❓ "If this had gone wrong, what exactly would have broken, and how far would it spread?"
items.explanation: Blast radius is a concrete way of asking about scope: if a given piece of work had gone wrong, what exactly would have broken and how far would the consequences have spread.

items.prompt: In L2's scope-estimation flowchart, what's the first question asked once a bug or task is identified?
choices: How long will the fix take?
Who else depends on this being right?
Is this technically difficult to fix?
Has this bug happened before?
items.reference:
1️⃣ Who else depends on this being right?
2️⃣ What happens if this stays wrong?
3️⃣ Contained/reversible → medium scope; spreads/hard to reverse → large scope, flag immediately
items.explanation: The flowchart's first branch point is "who else depends on this being right?" — this is the question that starts separating small-scope issues (nobody yet, isolated) from ones that need further investigation.

items.prompt: Per L2's flowchart, what distinguishes "medium scope" from "large scope" once other systems or teams do depend on the bug being right?
choices: Medium scope means nobody depends on it at all
Whether the failure, if it stays wrong, is contained and easy to reverse (medium) versus spreading, compounding, or hard to reverse (large)
Medium scope always takes longer to fix than large scope
There's no distinction — medium and large scope are treated identically
items.reference:
1️⃣ Who else depends on this being right?
2️⃣ What happens if this stays wrong?
3️⃣ Contained/reversible → medium scope; spreads/hard to reverse → large scope, flag immediately
items.explanation: The flowchart splits medium from large scope based on reversibility and spread: a contained, easily-reversed failure is medium scope, while one that spreads, compounds, or is hard to reverse is large scope — and large scope is the branch that calls for immediately flagging the risk to others.

items.prompt: L2 says Sam's catch read as senior partly because of WHEN a certain question was asked. What was that timing?

The question was never actually asked — it was pure luck

items.reference:
1️⃣ Who else depends on this being right?
2️⃣ What happens if this stays wrong?
3️⃣ Contained/reversible → medium scope; spreads/hard to reverse → large scope, flag immediately
items.explanation: L2 is explicit: Sam asked "what happens if this stays wrong" proactively, three weeks before the batch job ran — not reactively after a customer complaint forced the investigation, which is what made the catch preventive rather than reparative.

There's no connection between Sam's fix and this argument
items.reference:
🔧 Difficulty — how much skill the fix required
📏 Scope — how much the outcome mattered
💡 Sam's fix: small difficulty, large scope — the two are independent
items.explanation: Sam's fix — a single conditional check — was small in difficulty despite being large in scope, which is exactly the evidence L2 uses to show difficulty and scope are independent variables, not the same thing measured two ways.

items.prompt: What made Sam's fix read as senior-level, according to L2, if not the difficulty of writing it?

The seniority Sam already held before finding the bug

🔧 Difficulty — how much skill the fix required
📏 Scope — how much the outcome mattered
💡 Sam's fix: small difficulty, large scope — the two are independent
items.explanation: L2 attributes the senior read to judgment — the willingness to look at something "routine" and trace its actual blast radius before it caused a problem — not to the technical difficulty of the fix itself, which was small.

items.prompt: According to L2, what happens to a genuinely hard fix applied to a tiny-scope problem?
choices: It automatically becomes large-scope because of the effort invested
It still reads as tiny-scope — difficulty alone doesn't change how much the outcome mattered

items.reference:
🔧 Difficulty — how much skill the fix required
📏 Scope — how much the outcome mattered
💡 Sam's fix: small difficulty, large scope — the two are independent
items.explanation: L2 is explicit: a genuinely hard fix to a tiny-scope problem still reads as tiny-scope, once someone traces out the actual consequences — difficulty doesn't inflate scope, and the two should be evaluated independently.

items.prompt: Does L2 argue that Priya's small-scope fix was a waste of effort?
choices: Yes — small-scope work should never be done
No — the fix was still worth doing (cleaner debug logs help future debugging); it just isn't the work to lead a promotion case with

The unit doesn't address whether small-scope work has value

✅ Small-scope work still has value
🚫 It just isn't the work to lead a promotion case with

items.prompt: What is the correct takeaway about small-scope work, per L2's failure-modes section?
choices: Treating small-scope work as wasted effort is itself listed as a failure mode to avoid
Small-scope work should always be deprioritized in favor of large-scope work
Small-scope work should be inflated in write-ups to sound more important
Small-scope work doesn't need to be tracked at all
items.reference:
✅ Small-scope work still has value
🚫 It just isn't the work to lead a promotion case with

items.prompt: L2 lists "assuming difficulty and scope move together" as a failure mode. Why is this listed as a mistake?
choices: Because some of the highest-scope catches are single-line fixes, and some of the most technically impressive work touches nothing that matters
Because difficulty and scope are actually the exact same measurement
Because scope can only be assessed after a task is fully difficult to complete
Because this assumption is always correct and shouldn't be listed as a failure mode
items.reference:
⚠️ Difficulty ≠ scope — they can move independently in either direction
⚠️ Waiting for impact to be realized wastes the chance to get credit for prevention
items.explanation: L2 explains this failure mode with exactly this reasoning: some of the highest-scope catches (like Sam's) are technically trivial, while some of the most technically impressive work has no real consequence if it's wrong — the two variables move independently.

items.prompt: L2 lists "waiting until impact is realized to describe it" as a failure mode. What does it recommend instead?
choices: Never describing impact at all, since it's unreliable
Estimating and describing scope before something actually breaks, since waiting for an incident wastes the chance to get credit for prevention
Only describing impact after a formal incident report is filed
Waiting exactly one quarter before mentioning any impact
items.reference:
⚠️ Difficulty ≠ scope — they can move independently in either direction
⚠️ Waiting for impact to be realized wastes the chance to get credit for prevention
items.explanation: L2 recommends estimating scope proactively, before an incident happens, since waiting until impact is realized (i.e., until something actually breaks) wastes the opportunity to get credit for preventing it in the first place — exactly what Sam did.

items.prompt: L3 says the lesson generalizes "in two directions at once." What are those two directions?
choices: One direction for junior engineers and one for senior engineers
One habit for the person doing the work (tracing consequences and making them visible) and one for the person writing about someone else's work (translating actions into prevented consequences)
One direction for technical tracks and one for non-technical tracks

✍️ Writing about the work: translate "what did they do" into "what would have happened without them"
items.explanation: L3 splits the lesson into two roles: as the person doing the work, build the habit of tracing consequences before something breaks and surfacing that reasoning; as the person writing about someone else's work, translate actions into prevented consequences — both carry the scope information forward.

Whether Priya should be fired for not predicting this outcome

There's no real tension — the answer is obviously the same either way

🙋 Doing the work: trace consequences before something breaks, make the reasoning visible
✍️ Writing about the work: translate "what did they do" into "what would have happened without them"
items.explanation: The extend-it question probes whether scope that only becomes visible later should retroactively change how the original moment was framed, or whether it should only affect how a subsequent write-up credits the now-visible consequence — a genuine open question the unit invites the reader to reason through rather than answering for them.

It produces no visible artifact and disappears from the record entirely unless actively described

items.reference:
🙋 Doing the work: trace consequences before something breaks, make the reasoning visible

items.explanation: L3's failure-modes table notes that a caught bug that never happened produces no visible artifact by default — since nothing actually broke, there's no incident report or outage to point to, so the prevention has to be actively described or it simply disappears from the record.

items.prompt: You corrected a wrong date before a school invitation went to 3,000 families. Which review note makes the scope visible without exaggerating?
choices: Fixed a typo.
Corrected the event date before the invitation was sent to 3,000 families, preventing many people from arriving on the wrong day.
Saved the whole school from disaster and proved I am the best organizer.
Worked very hard on the invitation.
items.reference: Scope = how far the mistake could have spread. Good scope writing names the affected people, money, systems, or reversibility.
items.explanation: The best note states the concrete reach and prevented consequence. It does not inflate the work with a self-assessment, and it does not hide the scope behind the tiny word "typo."
